reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Caused by a lesion of the midbrain tegmentum involving the red nucleus, supplied by paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral and basilar arteries
Combines an ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral involuntary movements such as tremor, chorea, or ataxia
The extrapyramidal signs arise from damage to the red nucleus and adjacent cerebellothalamic (dentatorubrothalamic) fibres
Contralateral limb ataxia and a coarse rubral (Holmes) tremor help distinguish it from the purely pyramidal Weber syndrome
Some patients also show contralateral hemiparesis if the lesion extends ventrally towards the cerebral peduncle
The ipsilateral third nerve palsy gives a dilated pupil, ptosis, and a down-and-out eye, as in other midbrain syndromes
It represents a tegmental crossed midbrain syndrome, intermediate in territory between Weber and Claude
reference.pathophysiology: Benedikt syndrome follows infarction or haemorrhage in the paramedian midbrain tegmentum, supplied by perforating branches of the posterior cerebral and basilar arteries. The lesion involves the oculomotor fascicles passing through the tegmentum, producing an ipsilateral third nerve palsy, together with the red nucleus and the crossing dentatorubrothalamic fibres, producing contralateral tremor, chorea, or ataxia. When damage extends ventrally to the medial lemniscus or corticospinal fibres, contralateral sensory loss or weakness may be added. The result is an alternating syndrome dominated by involuntary movements, contrasting with the pure hemiparesis of Weber syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Holmes tremor from other midbrain or thalamic lesions
Wilson disease or other causes of secondary movement disorder
Posterior communicating artery aneurysm with third nerve compression
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the midbrain tegmentum to localise the infarct
MR or CT angiography of the posterior circulation and circle of Willis
Detailed examination of tremor, ataxia, and pupillary function
Vascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
Copper studies where a metabolic movement disorder is suspected
Vessel wall imaging when basilar atherosclerosis or dissection is considered
redFlags: Pupil-involving third nerve palsy prompting exclusion of a compressive aneurysm
Declining consciousness suggesting extension into the reticular formation
Bilateral tegmental signs implying a larger paramedian midbrain event
Rapid deterioration indicating evolving basilar occlusion
reference.prognosis: The oculomotor palsy may recover partially, but the rubral tremor and ataxia are often persistent and disabling, and the movement disorder may respond only incompletely to symptomatic treatment.
pitfalls: Labelling the picture as Weber syndrome and missing the tegmental movement disorder
Attributing a pupil-involving third nerve palsy to microvascular disease without vascular imaging
Overlooking a delayed-onset Holmes tremor emerging weeks after the stroke
Failing to distinguish contralateral ataxia from weakness at the bedside
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
